cues.text: Born around 331 to a Christian family in Tagaste in North Africa, Monica was given in marriage while still young to Patricius, a pagan official of the town known for a violent temper, and to a mother-in-law of similar disposition under whose roof the young bride had also to live.

Monica bore this difficult household, we are told, not with resignation but with an active, patient virtue that in time won the genuine respect of her volatile husband, who never once, in all their years together, is recorded to have raised a hand against her — a restraint his neighbors marveled at, and one Monica herself attributed entirely to prayer and to the deliberate gentleness with which she answered every provocation.

Of the three children Monica bore, her eldest, Augustine , would become both her greatest joy and her longest sorrow: a brilliant, ambitious young man who fell in with the heretical Manichaean sect, took a mistress, fathered a son out of wedlock, and showed every sign of a mind and heart drifting further from the faith his mother had tried to instill.

Monica's response, across nearly two decades, was neither despair nor the harsh rejection a lesser mother might have chosen, but an unrelenting campaign of prayer, tears, and patient counsel, so persistent that a bishop she once consulted for advice is said to have told her simply: it is not possible that the son of so many tears should perish .
Following Her Son Across the Sea

When Augustine, without telling her, slipped away by ship to Rome to advance his career, Monica's grief did not turn to abandonment but to pursuit: she followed him first to Rome and then to Milan, where providence had placed, as bishop of that city, a preacher of extraordinary eloquence named Ambrose .

It was under Ambrose's preaching, and under his mother's unrelenting prayer, that Augustine's long resistance finally began, in the famous garden scene he would later immortalize in his Confessions , to give way — a conversion Monica had prayed for through more years and more tears than most mothers are ever asked to give.
Augustine was baptized by Ambrose at the Easter Vigil of 387, Monica present to witness what she would later say was the one thing left in this world she had ever truly wanted.

In the months that followed, mother and son shared a period of deep spiritual conversation at Ostia, awaiting a ship back to Africa, in a scene of shared mystical contemplation Augustine records with unforgettable tenderness in his Confessions — mother and son, for a brief moment, united not merely in blood but in the very vision of God they had both, in their different ways, spent so long seeking.
Monica fell ill and died at Ostia before the ship could sail, in the autumn of 387, at fifty-six years old.

Asked by her sons whether she feared to die so far from her native Africa, she answered, Augustine tells us, that nothing is far from God, and that she had no fear at all of where her body might be laid, for the Lord would know where to find her on the day of resurrection.

Monica's own sanctity has always been inseparable, in the Church's memory, from the sanctity of the son whose conversion she prayed for so long to see, and rightly so: for she teaches every parent, every spouse, every believer who has ever loved someone still far from God, that persistent, patient, unglamorous prayer — offered not for years but for decades if necessary — is never wasted, and that God's timing, however painfully slow it may feel to a mother's heart, is never in the end too late.
